q: How does a machine learning system differ from a program built on hand-crafted rules?
options: It learns patterns from data instead of following written rules
It follows fixed rules but runs them much faster than a person could
It stores every past example and replays the matching answer
It needs a person to write a new rule for every case
explain: Machine learning improves at a task by learning from data, usually historical. Hand-written rules are what it replaces.

q: An agent learns to play a game by trying moves and receiving rewards or penalties. Which type of machine learning is this?
options: Supervised learning
Reinforcement learning
Unsupervised learning
Rule-based programming
explain: Reinforcement learning is trial and error guided by rewards. Supervised learning needs labelled examples and unsupervised learning looks for structure.

q: Which of the following are core building blocks of a machine learning approach?
options: A written list of rules covering every possible case
A guarantee that the training data is free of bias
Evaluation that checks how well the model generalises
An objective or loss that says what is being optimised
An optimisation method that fits the model
explain: The building blocks are data, a model family, a loss, optimisation and evaluation. Data quality, bias and leakage still need care and are never guaranteed.

q: Spammers and fraudsters keep changing their behaviour. Why does machine learning cope better than fixed rules?
options: Fixed rules cannot be changed once they are written
The model never needs fresh data after the first training
The model can be retrained on new data without rewriting the logic
The model replaces data quality checks with probabilities
explain: Behaviour that changes over time is called concept drift, and retraining adapts the model to it. Rules can be edited, but a growing rule set becomes hard to manage.

q: In which situations is a simple rule or a verified algorithm better than machine learning?
options: Having very little data of poor quality
Needing clear, auditable reasons for each decision
Calculating a drug dose where errors are unacceptable
Calculating tax bands that follow exact written rules
Spotting complex fraud patterns in huge amounts of data
Adapting to customers whose behaviour keeps changing
explain: Deterministic logic, safety critical use, tiny data and a need for transparency all favour rules. Complex patterns and changing data are where machine learning helps.

q: A bank wants to predict whether a new applicant will default within 12 months, yes or no. What kind of task is this?
options: Regression, because default risk is a score
Regression, because the bank holds numeric data on applicants
Clustering, because applicants form natural groups
Classification, because the outcome is a category
explain: Default or no default is a category, so this is classification. Regression predicts a continuous value such as a price or a time.

q: Which of the following are classification tasks?
options: Predicting wheat yield in tonnes per hectare
Forecasting a journey time in minutes
Deciding from a chest X-ray whether pneumonia is present
Labelling each customer as new, active or at risk of leaving
Identifying a dog's breed from a photo
explain: Classification predicts discrete classes. Yield and journey time are continuous numbers, which makes them regression.

q: Which of the following is a regression task?
options: Forecasting travel time in minutes for tomorrow morning
Deciding whether an email is spam
Deciding whether a customer will leave
Choosing a flower species from measurements
explain: Regression returns a numeric estimate of a continuous value. The other three produce a category.

q: A classifier outputs a probability for each class. How is this turned into a final label?
options: The model always picks the class seen most often in training
A threshold is chosen to balance the cost of false alarms and misses
The probabilities are averaged over all the training examples
A person reviews every prediction and picks the label
explain: The threshold is a decision made after the model produces its probabilities. Moving it trades false alarms against missed cases.

q: A fraud team has few investigators and wants most of its flagged cases to be real fraud. Which measure should it watch most closely?
options: Recall
Mean squared error
Precision
Accuracy
explain: Precision asks how many predicted positives are truly positive, so it matters when false positives are costly. Recall focuses on missed positives instead.

q: A hospital screening test must catch as many ill patients as possible, even at the cost of extra checks. Which measure matters most?
options: Precision
Accuracy
Specificity
Recall
explain: Recall is the share of actual positives that were caught, so it matters when missing a case is costly. Specificity concerns healthy people correctly cleared.

q: A model on a heavily imbalanced dataset always predicts the majority class. What will its accuracy look like?
options: High, even though it never finds a single positive case
Low, because it ignores half of the classes
Zero, because it never predicts the positive class
Equal to its recall on the positive class
explain: Accuracy counts all correct predictions, and the majority class makes up most of them. This is why accuracy can mislead and measures such as F1 are preferred.

q: Which statements about the confusion matrix are correct?
options: Precision and recall are derived from its four counts
It applies only to regression problems
It counts correct and incorrect predictions for each class
It records true negatives, which are correctly rejected cases
It records false negatives, which are missed positives
explain: The matrix holds true positives, false positives, true negatives and false negatives. It is a classification tool, so the regression option is wrong.

q: What does the F1 score combine?
options: Accuracy and specificity, using the arithmetic mean
Precision and recall, using the harmonic mean
Precision and specificity, using the median
Recall and specificity, using the harmonic mean
explain: F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, so it gives one balanced number. It is useful when classes are imbalanced.

q: What does an ROC curve plot as the decision threshold is varied?
options: Precision against the number of training examples
Accuracy against the number of neighbours used
The true positive rate against the false positive rate
Training loss against the number of passes over the data
explain: Each point on the curve is one threshold. AUC, the area under the curve, summarises how well the model ranks positives above negatives.

q: Which of the following correctly pair a classification algorithm with its description?
options: Support vector machines with a single tree of if then rules
Logistic regression with a linear classifier using a logistic function
Naive Bayes with a probabilistic method assuming independent features
k-NN with a model fitted fully before any prediction is made
Random forest with a bagged group of trees that reduces variance
explain: A single tree of if then rules describes a decision tree, not a support vector machine, which uses the kernel trick. k-NN does very little work until it is asked to predict.

q: Why can the same new point be given a different class when k is changed?
options: The distance measure changes whenever k changes
The training labels are rewritten for each new value of k
The model is retrained from scratch for every value of k
A different set of neighbours is counted, so the vote can change
explain: The neighbours counted at each k differ, so the majority may differ. The labels and the distance measure stay the same.

q: k-NN is called a lazy learner. What does this mean?
options: It does little work in training and most work when predicting
It learns very slowly and needs many passes over the data
It ignores some training examples to save effort
It makes predictions without comparing to any examples
explain: There is no real training phase. The cost comes at prediction time, when distances to the training points are computed.

q: How does k-NN give a prediction for regression instead of classification?
options: It takes a majority vote among the k nearest neighbours
It averages the values of the k nearest neighbours
It fits a straight line through all the training points
It averages the values of all training points, not just the nearest
explain: Classification uses a majority vote and regression uses an average of the neighbours' values. Both use the k nearest points.

q: A k-NN model uses age in years and income in pounds, left unscaled. What is the likely effect?
options: Age dominates the distance, because it is the smaller number
Both features count equally, because distance ignores units
Income dominates the distance, so age has little influence
The model cannot be fitted until the features are scaled
explain: Distance is driven by the feature with the largest numeric range, here income in pounds. Scaling puts features on a comparable footing.
flag: The slides state that k-NN is sensitive to irrelevant features and the Week 1 slides mention scaling for distance models. The unscaled income example is standard textbook knowledge.

q: Which of the following are drawbacks of k-NN?
options: It must assume the data follow a normal distribution
High memory and computation cost on large datasets
Performance depends heavily on the choice of k
It can only be used for classification
Sensitivity to irrelevant features and noise
explain: The two wrong options fail because k-NN works for classification and regression, and because it is non-parametric it assumes no particular data distribution.

q: How should the best value of k be chosen?
options: Always use k equal to one, because it matches the closest point
Use the value that gives the best result on the training data
Pick the value that makes the number of votes even
Compare several values on validation data and keep the best
explain: Validation data shows how each k performs on unseen examples, and cross-validation makes the comparison more reliable. Judging on training data would favour k equal to one, which memorises the training set.

q: What does Gini impurity measure in a node of a decision tree?
options: How mixed the classes in the node are
How many features are left to split on
How deep the node sits in the tree
How many samples the node contains
explain: Gini impurity is the chance of mislabelling a random sample if it is labelled by the node's class mix. A pure node, where all samples share one class, has an impurity of zero.

q: In a weather dataset, a decision tree at the root finds that splitting on Windy gives purer child nodes than splitting on Outlook. Which does it choose?
options: Outlook, because it has more possible values
Windy, because it gives the larger reduction in impurity
Outlook, because it always comes first in the table
Windy, because binary features are always chosen first
explain: The tree tries each split and keeps the one with the greatest gain, meaning the largest drop in weighted impurity. The number of values a feature has does not decide this.

q: Which of the following are valid reasons for a decision tree to stop splitting?
options: The training data has been shuffled
The node still contains more than one class
No features remain to split on
A maximum depth has been reached
The node is pure
A minimum number of samples has been reached
explain: A tree stops when a node is pure, no features remain, or a limit such as maximum depth or minimum samples is reached. Shuffling the data and a node that still holds several classes are not reasons to stop.

q: A leaf contains more Yes examples than No examples but is not pure. What does the tree predict for a new case that reaches it?
options: No prediction, because only pure leaves can predict
The minority class, to be cautious about the majority
The majority class, with a probability from the class mix
A class chosen at random from the examples in the leaf
explain: An impure leaf still predicts its majority class. The share of that class gives an estimated probability.

q: Define machine learning and distinguish supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning.
model: Machine learning is a branch of AI where systems learn patterns from data, usually historical data, to improve at a task instead of relying on hand-crafted rules. In supervised learning the model learns from labelled examples. In unsupervised learning there are no labels and the aim is to find structure in the data. In reinforcement learning an agent learns by trial and error, guided by rewards.
points: Learns patterns from data and not from hand-crafted rules
Supervised uses labelled examples
Unsupervised discovers structure without labels
Reinforcement uses trial and error with rewards

q: Explain why machine learning is sometimes better than rule-based approaches, and describe when it should not be used.
model: Machine learning is better when patterns are complex, there are many edge cases, data changes over time or inputs are noisy. It can capture nonlinear interactions and be retrained as behaviour drifts instead of rewriting rules. It should not be used with tiny or poor data, where it will overfit. It is also unsuitable when exact rules exist, in safety critical work where errors are unacceptable, and when clear auditable reasoning is required.
points: Complex patterns, many edge cases or changing data favour machine learning
Retraining adapts to concept drift
Tiny or poor data causes overfitting
Deterministic, safety critical or transparent needs favour rules

q: Explain supervised learning, including features and labels, and give one example each of classification and regression.
model: Supervised learning trains a model on labelled historical data so it can predict outcomes for new, unseen cases. The data hold input features, also called predictors or independent variables, and an output label, also called the target or dependent variable. In classification the label is a discrete class, for example predicting whether an email is spam. In regression the label is a continuous number, for example predicting the price of a house.
points: Learns from labelled examples to predict unseen cases
Features are inputs and the label is the target
Classification predicts a category with a valid example
Regression predicts a continuous value with a valid example

q: Explain how a classification model turns its output into a decision and why the threshold matters.
model: A classification model learns patterns that separate the categories and outputs a probability for each class. To get a final label, a threshold is applied to those probabilities. The threshold is chosen to balance the real-world costs of mistakes. Lowering it catches more positives but raises false positives. Raising it does the opposite, so the choice depends on whether false alarms or missed cases are more costly.
points: Model outputs probabilities for each class
A threshold converts probabilities to labels
Threshold balances costs of false positives and false negatives
Describes the effect of raising or lowering it

q: Compare precision and recall and say when each matters most.
model: Precision asks, of the items predicted positive, how many are truly positive. It matters when false positives are costly, for example fraud investigations where staff time is limited. Recall asks, of all the real positives, how many were caught. It matters when missing a positive is costly, for example disease screening. The F1 score combines the two when a balance is needed.
points: Precision is the share of predicted positives that are correct
Recall is the share of actual positives that were found
Precision matters when false positives are costly with an example
Recall matters when false negatives are costly with an example

q: Explain why accuracy can be misleading on imbalanced data and what you could use instead.
model: Accuracy is the share of all predictions that are correct. When one class is far more common, a model can predict that class every time and still score high accuracy while finding none of the rare cases. This hides poor performance on the class that usually matters. Better choices are precision, recall and the F1 score, and the confusion matrix shows where the mistakes fall.
points: Accuracy counts all correct predictions
A majority class guesser can look accurate
It hides failure on the rare class
Suggests precision, recall, F1 or the confusion matrix

q: Describe how k-NN classifies a new data point and explain why it is called lazy and non-parametric.
model: To classify a new point, k-NN chooses a value for k and measures the distance from the new point to the training points, for example with Euclidean distance. It takes the k nearest points and uses a majority vote of their classes. It is called lazy because it does little work during training and does most of its work at prediction time. It is non-parametric because it does not assume any underlying data distribution.
points: Choose k and measure distances to training points
Uses a majority vote of the k nearest neighbours
Lazy means little training and most work at prediction
Non-parametric means no assumed data distribution

q: Explain how you would choose a good value of k for a k-NN model.
model: The value of k strongly affects performance, so it should be chosen with evidence. Split the data into training and validation sets. Try several values of k, perhaps around an initial estimate. Measure each with a suitable performance metric on the validation data. Choose the value that performs best, and use cross-validation if you want a more reliable comparison. Judging on the training data alone would be misleading because it does not show how the model copes with unseen cases.
points: Performance depends heavily on k
Use training and validation sets
Compare several values with a metric
Pick the best and optionally use cross-validation

q: Explain how a decision tree decides which feature to split on.
model: A decision tree tries each possible split at a node and measures how pure the resulting child nodes are. Gini impurity shows how mixed the classes in a node are, and zero means all samples share one class. The tree calculates the weighted impurity of the children and compares it with the parent. The split with the largest drop, called the gain, is chosen. The same process then repeats on each child node.
points: Tries each possible split
Gini impurity measures how mixed a node is
Compares weighted child impurity with the parent to find the gain
Picks the split with the largest gain and repeats on the children

q: Describe when a decision tree stops growing and how it makes a prediction for a new case.
model: A tree stops splitting when nodes are pure, when no features remain, or when limits such as minimum samples or maximum depth are reached. To predict, a new case starts at the root and follows the branch matching each feature value until it reaches a leaf. The leaf gives the predicted class, which is the majority class there. An impure leaf also gives an estimated probability based on its class mix. For example, a leaf holding mostly Yes examples predicts Yes with a probability that reflects how many of its examples were Yes.
points: Stops when nodes are pure, features run out or limits are met
New case follows branches from the root to a leaf
Leaf predicts the majority class
Impure leaf gives an estimated probability
